problemes.titol: Per què el narrador estava emocionat per l'entrevista
problemes.text:
**THE DAY I MET THE STRANGE AND INSCRUTABLE STEVE JOBS**

One morning in Paris six years ago, I found myself sitting opposite Steve Jobs. I was feeling really excited, as getting an interview with Jobs had become an obsession. In recent years, particularly since his health had declined, he had rarely talked directly to the media. But then, one day I got the news: I’d been given an interview.

Over the years I’d built up a vague impression of what I could expect: there were stories about the notorious “**flamethrower** treatment” that he would give to anyone who made a mistake. Beyond this, I expected him to be something like the other captains of industry that I had come across, with magnetic personalities and enormous presence.

However, the reality turned out to be very different. The interview took place at Apple’s Paris Expo, an exhibition of the company’s latest technology. Once he had finished taking questions from the media I was asked to accompany him on a walk around the Expo. Like everything else in Jobs’ life, the program was meant to be strictly managed: a quick turn around the **show floor**, and then downstairs to his temporary office for our interview. But as soon as Jobs began his walk, a wild group of Apple fans suddenly appeared, shouting his name and surrounding us. Jobs visibly **shrank** as they approached. His bodyguards quickly took him downstairs. A public relations officer invited me to follow him. Suddenly I was in a room with the man I’d been running after for years. But it wasn’t what I expected at all. Yes, the man sitting in front of me looked like the Steve Jobs I knew. But the Steve Jobs I was used to seeing was always in command, always in control, when launching new products. This one, however, seemed frightened and a little confused.

We had half an hour scheduled to talk. I kept looking up at the clock. His assistant indicated that he still needed time to **settle**. Clearly disturbed by his brief encounter with the real world, he came to sit opposite me and adopted a defensive posture. Although we talked for 30 minutes, it wasn’t a fluent and easy conversation. He spent too much of his time avoiding questions that he felt were inappropriate. I asked him about Apple’s environmental policy, which had received some criticism recently. He rejected the **claim** that Apple’s products were less green than its rivals with the same argument that he had always used in press conferences. When I pushed for more details he simply refused to go any further.

I mentioned his health. It was a year after he had had a pancreatic cancer operation, and it seemed that he had beaten the disease successfully. He refused to give me any details about it. For most of my time with him, it seemed he just wasn’t mentally in the room. My presence seemed to be another reminder that not everything could be controlled.

This was, after all, a man whose life was so carefully organized that he rarely had to do anything that he didn’t want to. He used to spend most of his life in or around Apple’s headquarters in Silicon Valley. He followed a strict routine. He was so used to getting his way that when his cancer first appeared he tried to beat it simply through focusing on a diet of fruit and vegetables. It didn’t work.

All in all, I was supposed to have just met the most attractive character that the business world has seen in decades. In person, Steve Jobs turned out to be the most inscrutable and peculiar **entrepreneur** I’d ever interviewed.

*Text adapted from The Times (August 27, 2011)*

- **show floor**: pavelló firal / pabellón ferial
- **shrank**: encongir-se / encogerse
- **settle**: calmar-se / calmarse
- **claim**: acusació / acusación
- **entrepreneur**: empresari / empresario

problemes.enunciat:

[4 points]

**Topic 1.** Imagine you are a journalist who had the chance to interview Steve Jobs, asking him questions about his life and his technological products. Write down that dialogue.

passos.cos: Opció 1 del writing (cal triar-ne una de les dues): un **diàleg** en forma d'entrevista entre tu (periodista) i Steve Jobs. Mínim 100 paraules (apunta a 140-170; uns 25-30 minuts). La consigna demana preguntes sobre **dues coses**: la seva **vida** i els seus **productes tecnològics**: cobreix-les totes dues. Format: nom de qui parla + dos punts a cada torn. Pots aprofitar dades del reading (càncer, rutina, fans, medi ambient), però **no copiïs** frases del text.

Estructura de l'entrevista:

1. **Salutació i agraïment** (*Thank you for agreeing to talk to me*).
2. **Preguntes sobre la vida**: els inicis (el garatge, Apple el 1976), la salut, la rutina.
3. **Preguntes sobre els productes**: Mac, iPod, iPhone, iPad; què els fa especials.
4. **Una pregunta incòmoda** (medi ambient) i la reacció de Jobs, coherent amb el text.
5. **Tancament**: el futur i comiat.

**Estructures i connectors útils**

- Preguntes directes ben formades: *What made you…?, How did you feel when…?, Why do you think…?, Could you tell us…?*
- Passat simple i *used to* per a la biografia: *We started Apple in a garage*.
- Present perfect per a l'experiència: *You have changed the way we…*
- Expressions de l'entrevista: *To begin with…, Moving on to…, One last question…, Thank you for your time.*

**Journalist:** Mr Jobs, thank you for agreeing to talk to me. To begin with, how did it all start?

**Jobs:** Steve Wozniak and I founded Apple in my parents’ garage in 1976. We had no money, but we had a dream: to put a computer on every desk.

**Journalist:** You were fired from your own company in 1985. How did you feel?

**Jobs:** It was terrible, but it was probably the best thing that ever happened to me. It made me more creative.

**Journalist:** Moving on to your products, why do you think the iPhone has been so successful?

**Jobs:** Because it is simple. People don’t want instructions; they want things that just work.

**Journalist:** Some people say Apple’s products are not very green. What do you think?

**Jobs:** I’ve answered that question many times. Our products are as green as any others.

**Journalist:** One last question. How is your health?

**Jobs:** I’d rather not talk about that. Thank you for your time.

**Is it possible to live without computers nowadays?**

Computers have become part of almost everything we do. In my opinion, it is technically possible to live without them, but it would be extremely difficult.

Firstly, computers are everywhere, even when we cannot see them. Banks, hospitals, schools and supermarkets all depend on them. For example, if you want to make an appointment with the doctor or apply for a job, you usually need to do it online.

On the other hand, some elderly people still live happily without a computer. However, they normally rely on their children or grandchildren to do many things for them, such as paying bills or buying tickets.

Moreover, young people use computers to study, work and keep in touch with their friends. If computers disappeared, our lives would change completely.

To sum up, although it is possible to live without a computer at home, nobody can really escape from them in today’s society.

**Topic 1.** Write an opinion essay about how the use of the internet has changed our lives.

passos.cos: Opció 1 del writing (cal triar-ne una de les dues): un **opinion essay** sobre com l'ús d'internet ha canviat les nostres vides. Mínim 100 paraules (apunta a 140-170; uns 25-30 minuts). No n'hi ha prou amb fer una llista de canvis: cal **valorar-los** (positius, negatius o tots dos) i donar una opinió clara amb exemples. Registre neutre o formal.

Estructura en 4 paràgrafs:

1. **Introducció**: internet és a tot arreu; tesi (p. ex.: ens ha canviat la vida sobretot per a bé, però amb riscos).
2. **Canvis positius**: comunicació, informació, compres i tràmits, estudis.
3. **Canvis negatius**: addicció, privacitat (connecta amb el reading: el que deixem a la xarxa fins i tot després de morir), menys contacte cara a cara.
4. **Conclusió**: reafirma l'opinió.

**Estructures i connectors útils**

- Present perfect per als canvis: *The internet has changed…, We have become…*
- *used to* per al passat: *People used to write letters*.
- Comparatius: *faster, easier, more convenient than…*
- Connectors: *Firstly, In addition, However, On the other hand, To sum up*.

**How the internet has changed our lives**

In just twenty years, the internet has transformed the way we live. In my opinion, these changes have been mostly positive, although they also have some dangers.

Firstly, communication has become faster and cheaper. People used to write letters that took days to arrive, but now we can talk to friends on the other side of the world instantly. In addition, we can find any information in seconds, buy almost anything without leaving home and study online.

However, there is a negative side. Many teenagers spend hours on social networks and see their friends less often face to face. Moreover, we leave so much personal information online that our privacy is in danger, even after we die.

To sum up, I believe the internet has made our lives easier and more interesting, but we must learn to use it responsibly.

**Anna:** That’s true, but they promise to store everything safely. Besides, I love the idea of recording a goodbye video for my friends.

**Tom:** To be honest, I find it a bit creepy. I’d rather my private messages disappeared with me.

**Anna:** Fair enough. I guess it depends on each person.

problemes.transcripcio:
**Journalist:** With us today is Chris Ryan, a student of Spanish Studies at the University of Lleida, who grew up in one of the world’s remotest nations, Greenland. Today we would like to learn more about Greenland and Greenlandic life.

*[Now listen to the rest of the interview.]*

**Journalist:** Good morning, Chris.

**Chris:** Good morning.

**Journalist:** Why did you choose the University of Lleida for your studies?

**Chris:** Well, you know Greenland is all about ice. The ice sheet covers about 80% of the landmass. Spain is just the opposite: sun, sun and more sun. Besides, every summer holiday we took a vacation in Spain, because my grandparents used to live in Lleida.

**Journalist:** What is your experience of Europe?

**Chris:** Europe has so much. It has trees and warm weather, which I’m not used to. I can’t cope well with warm weather. So when I am in Spain, I feel it’s really, really hot.

**Journalist:** But how hot is hot? Do you mean twenty degrees Celsius? What do you do when it’s thirty degrees?

**Chris:** I just can’t deal with that kind of heat. I think twenty degrees is really hot for me. That’s the temperature in summer in Greenland! In Greenland, you don’t walk around in T-shirts and shorts and stuff like that. I always feel kind of uncomfortable if I have to dress for warm weather. I’m always hot in Spain. I’ve never been in Lleida in July when it’s 35º! *(laughs)*

**Journalist:** How are the winters back home?

**Chris:** Well, there’s a lot of snow, and if there’s too much snow, you can’t go to work. In most parts of Spain, as soon as there’re five centimeters of snow, everything stops, because people aren’t used to driving around in the snow. But up in Greenland it would have to be really wild before anything closed. Snowplows are driving around all the time.

**Journalist:** What’s the name of the town you lived in?

**Chris:** Nuuk. It’s the capital city. It’s the largest city in Greenland. When I lived there it was about thirteen thousand in population, and I think now they’re up to about fifteen thousand.

**Journalist:** Did you ever find it boring?

**Chris:** Living up there? No. I don’t think so, though we looked forward to our vacation in Spain, because in Greenland, movies and clothes are like a year back. When we came to Spain, we got the newest clothes. But I was happy in Greenland.

**Journalist:** And how do you feel about it now?

**Chris:** Now I’ve lived in Spain almost as long as I lived in Greenland, and it’s almost like another part of my life, because everything’s changed, and there’s so much more to do in Spain.

**Journalist:** Did you people in Nuuk drive around in snowmobiles shooting at wolves?

**Chris:** Well, there weren’t snowmobiles—well, there were, but mainly, there were dog sleds. We actually don’t shoot wolves, but we used to shoot a lot of other animals for example, reindeer. In fact, in Nuuk, you’re not allowed to ride a dog sled. You’ve got to go further north, because the dogs can be really dangerous.

**Journalist:** The sled dogs?

**Chris:** Yes. There are not many places in the city where you can have your twelve dogs, because they are so dangerous. They are really cute as puppies, but they aren’t treated as pets. problemes.transcripcio:
**Journalist:** With us today is Chris Ryan, a student of Spanish Studies at the University of Lleida, who grew up in one of the world’s remotest nations, Greenland. Today we would like to learn more about Greenland and Greenlandic life.

*[Now listen to the rest of the interview.]*

**Journalist:** Good morning, Chris.

**Chris:** Good morning.

**Journalist:** Why did you choose the University of Lleida for your studies?

**Chris:** Well, you know Greenland is all about ice. The ice sheet covers about 80% of the landmass. Spain is just the opposite: sun, sun and more sun. Besides, every summer holiday we took a vacation in Spain, because my grandparents used to live in Lleida.

**Journalist:** What is your experience of Europe?

**Chris:** Europe has so much. It has trees and warm weather, which I’m not used to. I can’t cope well with warm weather. So when I am in Spain, I feel it’s really, really hot.

**Journalist:** But how hot is hot? Do you mean twenty degrees Celsius? What do you do when it’s thirty degrees?

**Chris:** I just can’t deal with that kind of heat. I think twenty degrees is really hot for me. That’s the temperature in summer in Greenland! In Greenland, you don’t walk around in T-shirts and shorts and stuff like that. I always feel kind of uncomfortable if I have to dress for warm weather. I’m always hot in Spain. I’ve never been in Lleida in July when it’s 35º! *(laughs)*

**Journalist:** How are the winters back home?

**Chris:** Well, there’s a lot of snow, and if there’s too much snow, you can’t go to work. In most parts of Spain, as soon as there’re five centimeters of snow, everything stops, because people aren’t used to driving around in the snow. But up in Greenland it would have to be really wild before anything closed. Snowplows are driving around all the time.

**Journalist:** What’s the name of the town you lived in?

**Chris:** Nuuk. It’s the capital city. It’s the largest city in Greenland. When I lived there it was about thirteen thousand in population, and I think now they’re up to about fifteen thousand.

**Journalist:** Did you ever find it boring?

**Chris:** Living up there? No. I don’t think so, though we looked forward to our vacation in Spain, because in Greenland, movies and clothes are like a year back. When we came to Spain, we got the newest clothes. But I was happy in Greenland.

**Journalist:** And how do you feel about it now?

**Chris:** Now I’ve lived in Spain almost as long as I lived in Greenland, and it’s almost like another part of my life, because everything’s changed, and there’s so much more to do in Spain.

**Journalist:** Did you people in Nuuk drive around in snowmobiles shooting at wolves?

**Chris:** Well, there weren’t snowmobiles—well, there were, but mainly, there were dog sleds. We actually don’t shoot wolves, but we used to shoot a lot of other animals for example, reindeer. In fact, in Nuuk, you’re not allowed to ride a dog sled. You’ve got to go further north, because the dogs can be really dangerous.

**Journalist:** The sled dogs?

**Chris:** Yes. There are not many places in the city where you can have your twelve dogs, because they are so dangerous. They are really cute as puppies, but they aren’t treated as pets. They are work dogs. The owners, of course, respect them and love them. But you don’t go out and pet them. Small children might get killed if they came too close.

**Journalist:** Did you go riding on dog sleds?

**Chris:** No. No, I never tried it. In Nuuk, it’s something the tourists do. But not a lot of us did, because we had to go to another city. And to go to another city, you had to take a helicopter— no roads.

**Journalist:** Was there a hospital in Nuuk? What would you do if you got ill?

**Chris:** There’s a big hospital, actually, with the latest equipment. However, emergencies are flown into Denmark, but it’s a four-hour flight. So it has to be really bad to decide to fly to Denmark. Actually, in Greenland, doctors and nurses are often Danish. Because, I don’t know, it seems there aren’t enough Greenlandic doctors.

**Journalist:** Right, Denmark exports medical interns to Greenland.

**Chris:** Yes, and there’re teachers that go there, too. And also, I think that when you come up there as a Dane, it pays really well. And there are not many places to spend the money. But it’s also a bit expensive to live in Greenland, for example if you want to get fresh vegetables. A cucumber can easily cost four or five euro!

**Journalist:** What’s the strangest thing that you thought was normal, when you were growing up in Greenland?

**Chris:** Well, there’re some things, yeah! When you thought something was cute, like a little child, for instance, you took your nose to the little child, and you sniffed. And said, *Iggu, igg’*.

**Journalist:** What does that mean?

**Chris:** It means, yeah, Yum, cute.

**Journalist:** You smelled the kid. What else?

**Chris:** On your birthday, they wake you up by shouting that you stink. Also, you are given a lot of spare change, and you throw your coins up in the air, and you yell, *Bagga*. And then all the little children get to collect the coins. Like if you had a piñata and candy, but in Greenland, it’s money. I don’t know why.

**Journalist:** Last recollections?

**Chris:** In winter when we played outside there would often be Northern Lights. Which was both beautiful and frightening because it really made you feel so tiny, and also because we couldn’t help ourselves testing the ‘spirits’ by whistling. A local myth says that the Northern Lights are dead spirits who are playing with a ball which is in fact a head–if you whistle while they play, they will come for you.

**Journalist:** That’s very interesting. Thanks a lot, Chris. It’s been a pleasure.
